report.headline: Usage rate projected to fall from 24.7% to 19.5%, landing near the NBA average of 20.1%, while the efficiency projection is unreliable and both carry wide uncertainty bands

projection.text: Player A's usage rate is projected to decline from 24.7% in the 2012-13 EuroLeague season to 19.5% in the 2013-14 NBA season, close to the league-average usage rate of 20.1% that season.

risks.text: Turnover rate was 17.3% in the source season, a meaningful cost given the ball-handling load implied by the 25.8% assist rate.
The source-season sample is thin: only 29 games and 867 minutes.

The true shooting projection (52.5%) comes from a model that performs no better than simply guessing the league mean (both 4.7% MAE), so it carries no real information about efficiency in the new league.
The 80% interval for usage rate (14.6% to 24.3%) spans about two NBA standard deviations (4.8%), meaning the model cannot narrow Player A's likely role beyond a wide range around average.

strengths.text: In the source season Player A posted a 25.8% assist rate and 4.693 assists per 75 possessions, indicating significant playmaking responsibility.
Source-season true shooting was 56.5%, essentially at the EuroLeague average (+0.06 sd), showing efficient scoring even while carrying a 24.7% usage rate.
The projected NBA usage rate of 19.5% sits within one standard deviation of the league average (20.1%, SD 4.8%), suggesting a plausible rotation role rather than a marginal one.

uncertainty.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage rate runs from 14.6% to 24.3%, a span of roughly two NBA usage standard deviations (SD 4.8%), so the model can only place Player A in a broad band around the average; the true shooting projection of 52.5% should not be trusted at all, since the model's error on that metric (4.7%) is no better than the trivial league-mean baseline (also 4.7%).
